questions.questionText: A sample of water contains dissolved sodium chloride and a small amount of insoluble sand. Describe a suitable sequence of separation methods and explain the scientific principle used at each stage. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A school laboratory.
questions.explanation: Use filtration first to remove insoluble sand because the solid particles are retained by the filter while the solution passes through. Then use simple distillation to obtain pure water; water is vaporised and condensed while dissolved salt remains in the flask. If the aim is to recover the salt instead, evaporate the water or crystallise the salt solution, using controlled heating.

questions.questionText: An element X has atomic number 13 and mass number 27. State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of X, and explain how an ion X3+ forms. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A small-scale water-treatment investigation.
questions.explanation: Protons = 13. Neutrons = 27 − 13 = 14. A neutral atom has 13 electrons. X3+ forms when three electrons are removed, leaving 10 electrons.

questions.questionText: Explain why magnesium oxide has a high melting point and why molten magnesium oxide conducts electricity whereas solid magnesium oxide does not. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: An industrial chemistry exercise.
questions.explanation: MgO has a giant ionic lattice containing strong electrostatic attractions between Mg2+ and O2− ions, requiring much energy to overcome. In the solid the ions are fixed in position and cannot carry charge through the lattice. When molten, the ions are mobile and can carry electrical charge.

questions.questionText: Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. Calculate the amount, in moles, in 10.0 g of CaCO3 (Mr = 100), then calculate the volume of CO2 at r.t.p. produced if CaCO3 is in excess of acid. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A mining and manufacturing case study.
questions.explanation: Moles of CaCO3 = 10.0/100 = 0.100 mol. The equation gives a 1:1 mole ratio of CaCO3:CO2, so CO2 = 0.100 mol. At r.t.p. 1 mol gas occupies about 24 dm3, so volume = 0.100 × 24 = 2.40 dm3.

questions.questionText: A student reacts equal masses of calcium carbonate with excess hydrochloric acid. Experiment A uses large chips and Experiment B uses powder. Explain which experiment is faster and describe two other changes that could increase the rate. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A household chemistry investigation.
questions.explanation: Powder reacts faster because it exposes a larger surface area, producing more frequent successful collisions. Increasing temperature generally increases rate because particles have more kinetic energy and a greater fraction exceed activation energy. Increasing acid concentration also increases collision frequency; a suitable catalyst can speed some reactions by lowering activation energy.

questions.questionText: For the reversible reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), explain what happens to the equilibrium position when pressure is increased and why. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A school laboratory.
questions.explanation: The system shifts towards the side with fewer gas molecules. There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so increased pressure favours ammonia formation. The change does not alter the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature; it changes the equilibrium composition.

questions.questionText: Describe how a pure, dry sample of copper(II) sulfate crystals could be prepared from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Include the main practical steps. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A small-scale water-treatment investigation.
questions.explanation: Warm dilute sulfuric acid and add copper(II) oxide in small portions while stirring. Continue adding solid until some remains unreacted, showing the acid has been neutralised; filter off excess solid. Concentrate the filtrate by gentle evaporation, allow it to cool to crystallise, then filter and dry the crystals.

questions.questionText: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed. Identify the products at the cathode and anode and write half-equations for their formation. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: An industrial chemistry exercise.
questions.explanation: At the cathode, Pb2+ gains electrons: Pb2+ + 2e− → Pb. At the anode, bromide ions lose electrons: 2Br− → Br2 + 2e−. Lead forms at the negative electrode and bromine forms at the positive electrode.

questions.questionText: Explain why iron is extracted in a blast furnace using carbon monoxide and describe the role of limestone in the furnace. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A mining and manufacturing case study.
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide reduces iron(III) oxide to iron because it removes oxygen from the ore. Limestone decomposes on heating to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. Calcium oxide reacts with acidic impurities such as silica to form slag, helping separate impurities from molten iron.

questions.questionText: Ethanol can be oxidised to ethanoic acid. State the conditions generally used for this oxidation and explain one practical difference between complete combustion and controlled oxidation. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A household chemistry investigation.
questions.explanation: Ethanol can be oxidised using an oxidising agent such as acidified potassium manganate(VII), with heating; reflux is used when complete oxidation to the acid is required. Complete combustion in excess oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water. Controlled oxidation can form an oxygen-containing organic product such as ethanoic acid rather than fully oxidising all carbon to CO2.

questions.questionText: A sample of water contains dissolved sodium chloride and a small amount of insoluble sand. Describe a suitable sequence of separation methods and explain the scientific principle used at each stage. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A small-scale water-treatment investigation.
questions.explanation: Use filtration first to remove insoluble sand because the solid particles are retained by the filter while the solution passes through. Then use simple distillation to obtain pure water; water is vaporised and condensed while dissolved salt remains in the flask. If the aim is to recover the salt instead, evaporate the water or crystallise the salt solution, using controlled heating.

questions.questionText: An element X has atomic number 13 and mass number 27. State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of X, and explain how an ion X3+ forms. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: An industrial chemistry exercise.
questions.explanation: Protons = 13. Neutrons = 27 − 13 = 14. A neutral atom has 13 electrons. X3+ forms when three electrons are removed, leaving 10 electrons.

questions.questionText: Explain why magnesium oxide has a high melting point and why molten magnesium oxide conducts electricity whereas solid magnesium oxide does not. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A mining and manufacturing case study.
questions.explanation: MgO has a giant ionic lattice containing strong electrostatic attractions between Mg2+ and O2− ions, requiring much energy to overcome. In the solid the ions are fixed in position and cannot carry charge through the lattice. When molten, the ions are mobile and can carry electrical charge.

questions.questionText: Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. Calculate the amount, in moles, in 10.0 g of CaCO3 (Mr = 100), then calculate the volume of CO2 at r.t.p. produced if CaCO3 is in excess of acid. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A household chemistry investigation.
questions.explanation: Moles of CaCO3 = 10.0/100 = 0.100 mol. The equation gives a 1:1 mole ratio of CaCO3:CO2, so CO2 = 0.100 mol. At r.t.p. 1 mol gas occupies about 24 dm3, so volume = 0.100 × 24 = 2.40 dm3.

questions.questionText: A student reacts equal masses of calcium carbonate with excess hydrochloric acid. Experiment A uses large chips and Experiment B uses powder. Explain which experiment is faster and describe two other changes that could increase the rate. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A school laboratory.
questions.explanation: Powder reacts faster because it exposes a larger surface area, producing more frequent successful collisions. Increasing temperature generally increases rate because particles have more kinetic energy and a greater fraction exceed activation energy. Increasing acid concentration also increases collision frequency; a suitable catalyst can speed some reactions by lowering activation energy.

questions.questionText: For the reversible reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), explain what happens to the equilibrium position when pressure is increased and why. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A small-scale water-treatment investigation.
questions.explanation: The system shifts towards the side with fewer gas molecules. There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so increased pressure favours ammonia formation. The change does not alter the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature; it changes the equilibrium composition.

questions.questionText: Describe how a pure, dry sample of copper(II) sulfate crystals could be prepared from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Include the main practical steps. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: An industrial chemistry exercise.
questions.explanation: Warm dilute sulfuric acid and add copper(II) oxide in small portions while stirring. Continue adding solid until some remains unreacted, showing the acid has been neutralised; filter off excess solid. Concentrate the filtrate by gentle evaporation, allow it to cool to crystallise, then filter and dry the crystals.
